Napari-OmniEM is a napari plugin that provides a unified, GPU-accelerated interface for electron microscopy (EM) image processing. Built on EM-DINO and OmniEM , it brings foundation-model inference to practical, interactive workflows for diverse 2D and 3D EM datasets. Installation Getting Started Model Zoo Highlights Napari-OmniEM covers the full workflow, from inference to model management: Flexible inference with three modes: In-memory (tiled) for interactive work on data that fit in memory. Full Volume for single-pass inference without stitching seams. On-disk (local) for large volumes and multi-GPU inference. Task-aware model management : add, import, and share your own tasks and models. Shared backbone across tasks : one backbone is cached and reused by every loaded model, reducing GPU memory use. Tools workbench (🧰) : manage model memory, post-process Image-to-Image results, and view logs. It suits exploratory analysis, large-volume processing, and downstream quantitative studies. Feedback and support We welcome feature requests, workflow requirements, and bug reports. Visit the Napari-OmniEM repository to explore the source code, or open a GitHub issue to share feedback or report a problem. Related projects EM-SSL project OmniEM omniem-train

docs.text: Release Notes 0.3.0.1 On-disk inference streams every input. 2D, colour, and singleton-axis images now stream on-disk (bounded RAM, multi-GPU) instead of loading whole into memory. 0.3.0 Foundation-model core. The model lives in the published omniem package (EM-DINO ViT-L backbone). The plugin provides a lightweight, parity-verified interface to it. Custom tasks and models. Add your own Image-to-Image and Image-to-Label tasks through Preferences (⚙️) and import fine-tuned OmniEM checkpoints (full or head-only). Shared backbone and per-task heads. Weights are stored as one shared ViT-L backbone plus small per-task head files; full checkpoints are split automatically on import, and a backbone-management panel lets you inspect, rename, add, and remove backbones. Multi-GPU sliding-window inference with pre-inference GPU-memory estimates and out-of-memory-safe execution. Expanded Full Volume mode. The single-pass, seam-free mode introduced in 0.2.0 now covers both task types and integrates the pre-inference memory estimates. On-disk inference for large volumes that streams data with bounded RAM use. Image-to-Image post-processing. Rescale model output to the input's intensity range. GUI improvements. Reorganized Preferences and Tools dialogs, a single resize Scale (×) control for Image-to-Image output, and friendlier window sizing. 0.2.0 Full Volume inference. Single-pass, tile-artifact-free mode for in-memory data. Post-processing tools (🧰). Rescale output intensity. Logging. Write logs to ~/.napari-omniem/napari_omniem.log and open them with View Logs . Config-schema validation, atomic config writes, and tooltips throughout. 0.1.0 Initial release. In-memory and on-disk (large-volume) inference. Sliding-window tiled inference built on MONAI. OmniEM model with the EMDINOv1-ViT-L backbone. Built-in tasks: denoising, super-resolution, mitochondria segmentation. napari contributions: widget, .tif / .tiff reader, .npy writer, and EM sample data.

Importing Fine-tuned Models Napari-OmniEM can import compatible fine-tuned OmniEM heads through Add Solution . This page uses two example model families to show which artifacts you need and how to register them with the plugin. Models and required files This page demonstrates two model families from the omniem-train examples/ folder: Example Model purpose Task type Variants EMPIAR-11831 4× super-resolution Image-to-Image 2D ME2-Beta Mitochondria segmentation Image-to-Label 2D and 3D Prepare these items for each model variant: Item Purpose model.yaml Defines the OmniEM model and is selected as the model config in Add Solution . weights/head_best.pt Contains the task head selected for a Head-only import. Use each variant's config and head from the same model run. For ME2-Beta, the 2D and 3D variants require their own model.yaml and head_best.pt files. These examples use the default EMDINOv1-ViTL backbone ( 4246a479 ), which is already registered in Napari-OmniEM; no backbone weights are required. If a model uses a different backbone, follow Add a backbone before importing its head. Example 1: 4× super-resolution (Image-to-Image) Source: omniem-train/examples/EMPIAR-11831/ouputs/empair11931_sr4x/ (SBF-SEM tobacco tissue). The head restores detail lost to 4× downsampling. Its model.yaml : arch: omniemv1 encoder: emdinov1 img_z: 1 out_channels: 1 # one grayscale map kernel3d_z: null task_type: image2image resize4emdino: true Import it: Open Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Solutions , then select the existing Super-resolution task or create a compatible Image-to-Image task. Click Add Solution , then Select model config and pick the run's model.yaml . Choose the Head-only strategy, select weights/head_best.pt , and pair it with EMDINOv1-ViTL . Confirm. The head is copied into the managed weights folder and the solution appears in the task. Use it: run the imported model like any Image-to-Image solution; see In-memory inference . This head was trained for 4× super-resolution, so set Scale (×) <= 4.0 to use its intended factor. Example 2: mitochondria segmentation (Image-to-Label) Source: omniem-train/examples/ME2-Beta (FIB-SEM data from the MitoEM 2.0 benchmark). The head maps each EM image to a two-class mask: background ( 0 ) and mitochondria ( 1 ). The example provides two configurations for the same data: Variant img_z kernel3d_z Sample shape 2D ( run_mito_2d ) 1 null 224 × 224 × 1 3D ( run_mito_3d ) 16 3 224 × 224 × 16 The 2D model.yaml : arch: omniemv1 encoder: emdinov1 img_z: 1 out_channels: 2 # background + mitochondria kernel3d_z: null task_type: image2label resize4emdino: false Import it: Select the existing Mitochondria Segmentation task. Its Background and Mitochondria labels match out_channels: 2 . Click Add Solution , select the run's model.yaml , choose Head-only , pick weights/head_best.pt , and pair it with EMDINOv1-ViTL . Confirm. Repeat with the 3D run's model.yaml + head_best.pt to add the 3D variant as a second solution (it needs z ≥ 16 ). Use it: run the imported model like any Image-to-Label solution. Its output is a mask with Background and Mitochondria labels. After importing Imported solutions behave like the built-in solutions: they appear in the Task and Solution menus for both in-memory and local inference, and you can export or share them. To manage the shared backbone they run on, see Backbone management . References Wickramanayake, J. S., & Czymmek, K. J. (2023). A conventional fixation volume electron microscopy protocol for plants. Methods in Cell Biology, 177 , 83-99. Liu, P. (2026). MitoEM 2.0: A Benchmark for Challenging 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation from EM Images [Dataset]. Zenodo.

docs.text: Multi-Task Inference: Super-Resolution + Segmentation Screenshots Screenshots on this page show the v0.2 interface and are pending update. Napari-OmniEM lets you chain models in a single analysis workflow. This example shows how applying super-resolution before segmentation can improve mitochondria segmentation compared with segmenting the original data directly (Figure 5 in the manuscript). The experiment uses a downsampled glycolytic-muscle EM dataset from CEM-MitoLab . The dataset is included with Napari-OmniEM as sample data. This page compares two workflows: Direct segmentation : segment mitochondria directly in the downsampled data. Super-resolution + segmentation : upsample the data first, then segment. Data Select File → Open Sample → OmniEM → EM to load the three bundled datasets. Use the GlyMuscle (3D) layer for this example. Open the OmniEM panel and select the layer from the Data list. Set the z-dimension to 0 , then open the Image Properties panel and verify that the data shape is [302, 168, 336] . Direct Mitochondria Segmentation Select Mitochondria Segmentation from the Task list. We recommend the ViT-L-2D solution for its stronger generalization. Adjust the settings as needed. For example, set the output name to raw-seg to identify the result and reduce the batch size to 1 to lower memory use. Click Run model and wait for the results. Super-Resolution Select Super-resolution from the Task list and set Scale (×) to 2.0 . This doubles both in-plane axes (168 → 336 and 336 → 672); the z-axis is not scaled. The panel displays the resulting output shape. Click Run model to start super-resolution inference. When the run finishes, remove any unused data layers and switch to Grid view to compare the results side by side. Mitochondria Segmentation on Super-Resolved Data Select the new super-resolution image from the Data list. Layers synchronize automatically; use 🔄 Synchronize Data only if the layer is missing. Select Mitochondria Segmentation as the task. To account for the higher input resolution, increase XY Input Size to a larger value, such as 448 . Click Run model and wait for the segmentation results. Switch to 3D view to compare the results more clearly. Conclusion Napari-OmniEM can chain complementary models within one interactive workflow. Here, super-resolution provides a higher-resolution input for mitochondria segmentation and can improve the final result. The same approach can adapt model sequences to other EM datasets and analysis goals. docs.text: Model Zoo All models in Napari-OmniEM use the OmniEM core architecture. OmniEM Architecture OmniEM is a unified framework for applying a consistent model architecture to multiple electron microscopy (EM) tasks. Model behavior depends on: Task type Input dimensionality Shared backbone, per-task heads Every model reuses one shared ViT-L backbone : the EM-DINO encoder (tag 4246a479 , shown in the GUI as EMDINOv1-ViTL ), plus a small per-task head . The backbone is loaded once and reused by every task that needs it. Running several models therefore does not reload the encoder, which reduces GPU memory use. Weights are stored in a managed folder as one shared backbone_<tag>.pt plus a head_*.pt per solution. See Backbone management and Custom model requirements . Task types Models are grouped by the GUI Task Type : Image-to-Image : the output is an image of the same kind as the input (for example, super-resolution or denoising). Image-to-Label : the output is a labeled mask (e.g. mitochondria). Dimensionality support OmniEM models can operate in either 2D or 3D mode. Model mode img_z Accept 2D Image Accept 3D Volume 2D 1 Yes Yes 3D > 1 No Yes Data type configuration The datatypes field defines the accepted input dimensionality: 2D data 3D data Available models Every built-in model is a small task-specific head on the shared EM-DINO ViT-L/14 backbone: Task Type Model Model context Required Z Trained on Backbone tag Head tag Denoising Image-to-Image emdiffuse-l 2D (slice-wise) ≥1 EMDiffuse (low-noise) 4246a479 e9638f8f Super-resolution Image-to-Image emdiffuse-l 2D (slice-wise) ≥1 EMDiffuse (low-level degradation) 4246a479 616dfcbc Mitochondria segmentation Image-to-Label ViT-L-2D 2D (slice-wise) ≥1 CEM-MitoLab 4246a479 7c18ec1e Mitochondria segmentation Image-to-Label ViT-L-3D 3D ≥16 MitoEM-R 4246a479 2c5f8505 Training and fine-tuning OmniEM To train or fine-tune OmniEM on your own dataset, use the omniem-train repository. Note To import an externally trained model into Napari-OmniEM, export compatible weights and configuration metadata.

docs.text: Mitochondria Segmentation Task type Image-to-Label Overview The Mitochondria Segmentation task classifies each pixel in an electron microscopy (EM) image. It provides a 2D slice-wise model trained on the CEM-MitoLab dataset and a volumetric 3D model trained on the MitoEM dataset . This task outputs a labeled mask with the following classes: Background Mitochondria Available solutions 1. ViT-L-2D Configuration - name: ViT-L-2D datatypes: [2, 3] img_z: 1 weights_head: head_mito-seg-ViT-L-2D.pt backbone_tag: 4246a479 head_tag: 7c18ec1e Characteristics img_z = 1 (2D model) Accepts: 2D input 3D input (processed slice by slice) No inter-slice fusion Suitable for fast inference and datasets without strong Z-continuity Recommended use cases 2D EM slice segmentation Large-scale screening Datasets with uncertain Z-alignment consistency 2. ViT-L-3D Configuration - name: ViT-L-3D datatypes: [3] img_z: 16 weights_head: head_mito-seg-ViT-L-3D.pt backbone_tag: 4246a479 head_tag: 2c5f8505 Characteristics img_z = 16 (3D model) Accepts 3D input only Requires a Z-dimension of at least 16 Full Volume and the 3D model With the ViT-L-3D model, Full Volume inference may produce boundary gaps between input blocks. docs.text: Custom model requirements Napari-OmniEM can run compatible models trained outside the plugin. This page describes the artifacts and model contract required for import. From a custom model to inference Follow this three-stage workflow: Prepare the task. Select an existing task with the correct task type, or create a new task . For an Image-to-Label model, define labels whose count and order match the model outputs. Add the solution. Prepare the config and weights according to the requirements on this page, then follow the Add Solution procedure to validate and register the model. Run inference. Select the registered task and solution, choose an appropriate inference mode, and follow the inference workflow . Compatibility overview A custom model must be compatible with the installed omniem package, which must be able to parse the model config and load the corresponding weights. OmniEM compatibility is necessary but not sufficient The omniem package may support models that the current Napari-OmniEM release has not enabled. Use the architecture and encoder listed under Required materials below. Required materials Prepare these materials from the same training or export run: A model using the omniemv1 architecture with the emdinov1 encoder. Other architectures cannot currently be imported into Napari-OmniEM. A model config ( .yaml or .yml ) that can be parsed by omniem.config.ModelConfig.from_yaml() . A compatible PyTorch weights file ( .pt ) in one of these layouts: A combined checkpoint containing the backbone and task head. A head-only checkpoint containing the metadata needed to identify its head and donor backbone. A matching backbone must already be registered in Napari-OmniEM; see Managing backbones . Use the config distributed with the selected weights. Do not reuse a config from another run simply because the architectures look similar. Keep the config and weights together A model config is not cryptographically tied to a checkpoint. A mismatched pair may pass basic file checks but fail during model loading or silently produce incorrect results. Model configuration Napari-OmniEM uses the model-config format defined and validated by the omniem package. Refer to the omniem documentation for the current configuration schema, field requirements, and examples. Use the config generated for the same training or export run as the selected weights. Preparation checklist Before opening Add Solution , confirm that: [ ] The config and weights came from the same training or export run. [ ] The config satisfies the requirements documented by omniem . [ ] The installed omniem package can load the model artifacts. [ ] The destination task type and labels match the model outputs. [ ] A head-only checkpoint has its matching backbone registered. Training and examples Use omniem-train to train or fine-tune compatible OmniEM heads. Keep the generated model config with its weights when transferring a run. Related pages Task, solution, and backbone management Inference Model Zoo Importing Fine-tuned Models

docs.text: Inference Napari-OmniEM offers two inference workflows: In-memory (main panel): the quickest way to run a model, best for interactive exploration and small-to-medium data that fits in memory. Local (on-disk) (📁 wizard): streams large volumes from disk with bounded memory and multi-GPU support. Task and solution selection and the sliding-window parameters work the same way in both workflows. See Tips & common pitfalls below. Choose an inference mode Use the size of your data and the required output quality to choose a mode: Choose data ├─ Too large to fit in memory or requires multiple GPUs │ └─ Local (on-disk) └─ Fits in memory ├─ Seam-free output needed and sufficient GPU memory available │ └─ Full Volume └─ Otherwise └─ In-memory (tiled) Select task and solution → Configure → Run → View or save Continue with in-memory tiled inference , Full Volume mode , or local on-disk inference . In-memory inference In-memory inference runs directly in the main Napari-OmniEM panel on data loaded as napari image layers. It is the quickest way to run a model and is best for interactive exploration, debugging, and small-to-medium EM datasets . Everything stays in memory The input volume, intermediate tiles, and result all occupy GPU or CPU memory during the run, so the available memory limits this mode. For volumes too large to hold in memory, use Local inference instead. You can run in one of two modes : Sliding window (default): splits the volume into overlapping tiles, runs each tile through the model, and stitches the results together. It uses less GPU memory and can handle larger inputs. Full Volume : the whole image is fed to the model in a single forward pass. Avoids stitching seams but needs more GPU memory. See Full Volume mode below. Select data Load image data into napari by selecting File → Open File(s) . The data appear as one or more Image layers. Loaded layers are detected automatically. If one is missing (rarely), click 🔄 Synchronize Data to rescan. Select the target image from the Data dropdown list. If the selected input is a 3D volume , specify the z-dimension : By default, Napari-OmniEM selects the axis with the shortest length . Change the selection if your data use a different axis convention. Select task and solution Choose the Task that corresponds to your processing goal: an Image-to-Image task (e.g. denoising, super-resolution) or an Image-to-Label task (e.g. mitochondria segmentation). Select a compatible Solution from the Solution list. The list is filtered automatically by the selected data: only solutions whose dimensionality and modality match the chosen layer are enabled, so you cannot select an incompatible model. Not sure which to choose? Click the 💡 button next to the Task or Solution dropdown to show its details. For more detailed descriptions of the built-in models, see the Model Zoo . Terminology A Task defines the problem to solve. A Solution is a specific model and configuration that solves that task. This terminology is consistent across in-memory and local inference. Output options by task type The panel shows different output controls depending on the task type: Image-to-Image : a single Scale (×) control (range 1.0–8.0, step 0.5). The ratio is applied to the in-plane (X/Y) axes together; the Z axis is never scaled. 1.0 keeps the size; restoration never downscales. The panel shows the resulting output shape as you adjust the value. Some models are trained for modest scaling. Image-to-Label : a read-only table showing the label → value mapping used in the output mask. No additional configuration is required. Advanced settings The Advanced section contains settings for the current run. Their defaults come from Preferences . If you are unsure which values to use, keep the defaults for your first run. Full Volume : enables Full Volume mode; see the next section . Sliding-window only (disabled in Full Volume mode): Overlap , Batch Size , XY Input Size : tiling controls; see Sliding Window Parameters . Blend mode : how overlapping tiles are combined ( constant or gaussian ). Both modes: Normalization source : scan-data (statistics measured over the whole volume) or model (the model's built-in statistics). Full Volume mode Tick Full Volume to feed the whole image to the model in a single forward pass instead of tiling. This avoids sliding-window stitching seams and works for both Image-to-Image and Image-to-Label tasks, but it uses more GPU memory. The sliding-window controls (overlap, batch size, XY input size, and blend mode) are disabled; the normalization setting still applies. If the input is not square, you are asked whether to use its height or width as the square input size. Napari-OmniEM restores the original aspect ratio and applies the requested output scale afterward; it does not crop the image. Run inference Click Run model to open the inference dialog. It shows the device, the planned work (either the batch count or padded input and output shapes), and the estimated GPU memory range for the run. Start the run from the dialog. When it finishes, the OK button becomes Redo so you can rerun with different settings. The result appears in napari as a new layer. For Image-to-Image results, you can rescale output intensity back to the input's range with the Post-process → Image-to-Image tool. Local (on-disk) inference Open local (on-disk) inference by clicking the 📁 button in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. Napari-OmniEM loads data from local files using dask.array and stores intermediate results are stored as temporary HDF5 files (more efficient backends are planned). It is a step-by-step wizard: Input Data → Task → Advanced settings → Run → Output. Open the panel Click the 📁 icon in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. This option is enabled only when a compatible GPU is available. Step 1: Select data Click Browse File to select a local image or volume. Common image formats read by dask-image are supported, such as TIFF (including multipage stacks, which load as 3D volumes), PNG , and JPEG . The data must be 2D (H, W) , 3D (Z, H, W) , or a colour variant (H, W, C) / (Z, H, W, C) ; other shapes are rejected. The model works on single-channel data. If you load a colour or multi-channel image, a Channel selector appears so you can reduce it to one channel: Convert to grayscale (weighted) (default): combine the colour channels into one grayscale channel. Extract single channel : keep one channel, chosen by its 0-based index . If the data are 3D, specify the z-dimension : By default, the axis with the shortest length is selected. Override this if your data use a different axis convention. Everything streams from disk Every input—2D, colour, or 3D—is processed as a streamed 3D volume with bounded memory use. Even large 2D images can therefore run without being loaded into memory in full. Step 2: Select task and solution Task and solution selection is the same as in in-memory inference. Incompatible tasks and solutions are shown but disabled. Step 3: Advanced settings (sliding window & devices) In addition to the standard sliding-window parameters, local inference provides: Device selection GPU-only inference; at least one GPU must be chosen. You can select multiple GPUs for parallel inference. Each selected GPU holds a complete model replica (backbone and head). The shared backbone is not deduplicated across GPUs, so total VRAM use increases in proportion to the number of GPUs. Normalization source : scan-data (whole-volume statistics), model (built-in statistics), or manual (enter mean/std yourself). Manual is offered only here, in the on-disk wizard. Temporary folder : where the scratch file is written during inference. Step 4: Run inference A persistent banner displays the run's estimated GPU memory requirement and the multi-GPU caveat described above. Click Run to start inference. When inference finishes, Run changes to Redo , so you can rerun with modified settings. Step 5: Save output Supported output options include: Open in napari Load the input data, the results, or both. Use this option cautiously with very large datasets. Standard file formats TIFF PNG (2D results only) NumPy ( .npy ) Chunked storage formats Zarr NumPyStack How local inference differs Compared with in-memory inference, local inference: Enables multi-GPU parallel inference when multiple GPUs are available. Writes a scratch file whose size is driven by the output : the pre-flight banner shows the estimate. Upscaling (Image-to-Image with Scale > 1) raises it substantially. Supports saving outputs in multiple formats , with optional visualization in napari. Cannot chain an Image-to-Image result into an Image-to-Label run in a single pass. Save the first result, then reload it for the second run. Does not offer Full Volume mode (that is an in-memory option). Tips & common pitfalls Shared guidance for both modes. For what each tiling control does, see Sliding Window Parameters . What uses memory The input volume, model, intermediate tiles, and result all require storage during inference. In-memory mode keeps them in RAM or VRAM; local mode streams the volume from disk and holds only a bounded working set. A higher Scale (×) , a larger XY input size , or Full Volume mode all raise the peak. If you run out of memory Try these in order: Reduce Batch Size (even 1 is acceptable). Reduce the XY input size . Lower the Scale (×) , or turn Full Volume off (in-memory). Switch to local inference , which streams data from disk. Balancing performance and memory Most controls trade memory for speed or quality, so pick the largest settings your hardware allows: A larger Batch Size raises throughput but uses more memory; it does not change output quality. A larger XY input size gives the model more context (often better results) at a higher memory cost. Full Volume avoids stitching seams but needs the most memory; sliding window trades a small seam risk for a much smaller footprint. Start from the defaults, then raise one setting at a time until you approach your memory limit. Shared backbone Models that use the same backbone keep one resident copy of it, so switching between such solutions does not reload the encoder and keeps GPU use low. See Task, solution, and backbone management . Memory warnings Before each run, the plugin estimates the required memory and compares it with the available GPU and CPU memory and your configured limits. If the run may not fit, the plugin warns you. You can adjust the settings or select Proceed anyway at your own risk. See memory limits in Preferences . Scratch disk (local inference) On-disk inference writes an output-sized scratch HDF5 file. Size the disk from the pre-flight banner, not a fixed rule of thumb; upscaling raises the requirement substantially. Temporary files are cleaned up on close An on-disk result is backed by a scratch HDF5 file so the whole volume never sits in RAM. Closing the Local Inference window deletes that window's scratch automatically ; results you opened into napari are in-memory copies and are kept. Use 🧰 → Memory Management → Clear temporal data only to remove leftovers from an interrupted run. Change the selection if your data use a different axis convention.
docs.title: Select data

docs.text: Choose the Task that corresponds to your processing goal: an Image-to-Image task (e.g. denoising, super-resolution) or an Image-to-Label task (e.g. mitochondria segmentation). Select a compatible Solution from the Solution list. The list is filtered automatically by the selected data: only solutions whose dimensionality and modality match the chosen layer are enabled, so you cannot select an incompatible model. Not sure which to choose? Click the 💡 button next to the Task or Solution dropdown to show its details. For more detailed descriptions of the built-in models, see the Model Zoo . Terminology A Task defines the problem to solve. A Solution is a specific model and configuration that solves that task. This terminology is consistent across in-memory and local inference.
docs.title: Select task and solution

docs.text: The panel shows different output controls depending on the task type: Image-to-Image : a single Scale (×) control (range 1.0–8.0, step 0.5). The ratio is applied to the in-plane (X/Y) axes together; the Z axis is never scaled. 1.0 keeps the size; restoration never downscales. The panel shows the resulting output shape as you adjust the value. Some models are trained for modest scaling. Image-to-Label : a read-only table showing the label → value mapping used in the output mask. No additional configuration is required.
docs.title: Output options by task type

docs.text: The Advanced section contains settings for the current run. Their defaults come from Preferences . If you are unsure which values to use, keep the defaults for your first run. Full Volume : enables Full Volume mode; see the next section . Sliding-window only (disabled in Full Volume mode): Overlap , Batch Size , XY Input Size : tiling controls; see Sliding Window Parameters . Blend mode : how overlapping tiles are combined ( constant or gaussian ). Both modes: Normalization source : scan-data (statistics measured over the whole volume) or model (the model's built-in statistics).
docs.title: Advanced settings

docs.text: Tick Full Volume to feed the whole image to the model in a single forward pass instead of tiling. This avoids sliding-window stitching seams and works for both Image-to-Image and Image-to-Label tasks, but it uses more GPU memory. The sliding-window controls (overlap, batch size, XY input size, and blend mode) are disabled; the normalization setting still applies. If the input is not square, you are asked whether to use its height or width as the square input size. Napari-OmniEM restores the original aspect ratio and applies the requested output scale afterward; it does not crop the image.
docs.title: Full Volume mode

docs.text: Click Run model to open the inference dialog. It shows the device, the planned work (either the batch count or padded input and output shapes), and the estimated GPU memory range for the run. Start the run from the dialog. When it finishes, the OK button becomes Redo so you can rerun with different settings. The result appears in napari as a new layer. For Image-to-Image results, you can rescale output intensity back to the input's range with the Post-process → Image-to-Image tool.
docs.title: Run inference

docs.text: Open local (on-disk) inference by clicking the 📁 button in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. Napari-OmniEM loads data from local files using dask.array and stores intermediate results are stored as temporary HDF5 files (more efficient backends are planned). It is a step-by-step wizard: Input Data → Task → Advanced settings → Run → Output.
docs.title: Local (on-disk) inference

docs.text: Click the 📁 icon in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. This option is enabled only when a compatible GPU is available.
docs.title: Open the panel

docs.text: Click Browse File to select a local image or volume. Common image formats read by dask-image are supported, such as TIFF (including multipage stacks, which load as 3D volumes), PNG , and JPEG . The data must be 2D (H, W) , 3D (Z, H, W) , or a colour variant (H, W, C) / (Z, H, W, C) ; other shapes are rejected. The model works on single-channel data. If you load a colour or multi-channel image, a Channel selector appears so you can reduce it to one channel: Convert to grayscale (weighted) (default): combine the colour channels into one grayscale channel. Extract single channel : keep one channel, chosen by its 0-based index . If the data are 3D, specify the z-dimension : By default, the axis with the shortest length is selected. Override this if your data use a different axis convention. Everything streams from disk Every input—2D, colour, or 3D—is processed as a streamed 3D volume with bounded memory use. Even large 2D images can therefore run without being loaded into memory in full.
docs.title: Step 1: Select data

docs.text: Task and solution selection is the same as in in-memory inference. Incompatible tasks and solutions are shown but disabled.
docs.title: Step 2: Select task and solution

docs.text: In addition to the standard sliding-window parameters, local inference provides: Device selection GPU-only inference; at least one GPU must be chosen. You can select multiple GPUs for parallel inference. Each selected GPU holds a complete model replica (backbone and head). The shared backbone is not deduplicated across GPUs, so total VRAM use increases in proportion to the number of GPUs. Normalization source : scan-data (whole-volume statistics), model (built-in statistics), or manual (enter mean/std yourself). Manual is offered only here, in the on-disk wizard. Temporary folder : where the scratch file is written during inference.
docs.title: Step 3: Advanced settings (sliding window & devices)

docs.text: A persistent banner displays the run's estimated GPU memory requirement and the multi-GPU caveat described above. Click Run to start inference. When inference finishes, Run changes to Redo , so you can rerun with modified settings.
docs.title: Step 4: Run inference

docs.text: Supported output options include: Open in napari Load the input data, the results, or both. Use this option cautiously with very large datasets. Standard file formats TIFF PNG (2D results only) NumPy ( .npy ) Chunked storage formats Zarr NumPyStack
docs.title: Step 5: Save output

docs.text: Compared with in-memory inference, local inference: Enables multi-GPU parallel inference when multiple GPUs are available. Writes a scratch file whose size is driven by the output : the pre-flight banner shows the estimate. Upscaling (Image-to-Image with Scale > 1) raises it substantially. Supports saving outputs in multiple formats , with optional visualization in napari. Cannot chain an Image-to-Image result into an Image-to-Label run in a single pass. Save the first result, then reload it for the second run. Does not offer Full Volume mode (that is an in-memory option).
docs.title: How local inference differs

docs.text: Shared guidance for both modes. For what each tiling control does, see Sliding Window Parameters .
docs.title: Tips & common pitfalls

docs.text: The input volume, model, intermediate tiles, and result all require storage during inference. In-memory mode keeps them in RAM or VRAM; local mode streams the volume from disk and holds only a bounded working set. A higher Scale (×) , a larger XY input size , or Full Volume mode all raise the peak.
docs.title: What uses memory

docs.text: Try these in order: Reduce Batch Size (even 1 is acceptable). Reduce the XY input size . Lower the Scale (×) , or turn Full Volume off (in-memory). Switch to local inference , which streams data from disk.
docs.title: If you run out of memory

docs.text: Most controls trade memory for speed or quality, so pick the largest settings your hardware allows: A larger Batch Size raises throughput but uses more memory; it does not change output quality. A larger XY input size gives the model more context (often better results) at a higher memory cost. Full Volume avoids stitching seams but needs the most memory; sliding window trades a small seam risk for a much smaller footprint. Start from the defaults, then raise one setting at a time until you approach your memory limit.
docs.title: Balancing performance and memory

docs.text: Models that use the same backbone keep one resident copy of it, so switching between such solutions does not reload the encoder and keeps GPU use low. See Task, solution, and backbone management .
docs.title: Shared backbone

docs.text: Before each run, the plugin estimates the required memory and compares it with the available GPU and CPU memory and your configured limits. If the run may not fit, the plugin warns you. You can adjust the settings or select Proceed anyway at your own risk. See memory limits in Preferences .
docs.title: Memory warnings

docs.text: On-disk inference writes an output-sized scratch HDF5 file. Size the disk from the pre-flight banner, not a fixed rule of thumb; upscaling raises the requirement substantially. Temporary files are cleaned up on close An on-disk result is backed by a scratch HDF5 file so the whole volume never sits in RAM. Closing the Local Inference window deletes that window's scratch automatically ; results you opened into napari are in-memory copies and are kept. Use 🧰 → Memory Management → Clear temporal data only to remove leftovers from an interrupted run.

docs.text: Installation Install Napari-OmniEM from source by cloning the repository, creating an environment, installing the plugin, and downloading the pretrained weights. 1. Clone the repository The code, configuration files, and example data are on GitHub: git clone https://github.com/pku-maleilab/napari-omniem.git cd napari-omniem 2. Create the environment and install the plugin Run these commands from the repository root (the napari-omniem/ directory you just cloned): # Create a new conda environment (Python 3.11 required) conda create -n napari-omniem python=3.11 conda activate napari-omniem # Install PyTorch first. Choose the command for your platform (CUDA version # or CPU) from the official selector: https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/ # Example (CUDA 11.8): pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118 # CPU-only alternative: # pip install torch torchvision torchaudio # Install the plugin in editable mode from the repository root. # Editable mode is required: the plugin loads weights from the # weights_split/ folder relative to the cloned repository (step 3). # This also pulls omniem from PyPI (a normal dependency). pip install -e . 3. Download the pre-trained weights The model weights are distributed separately. Download the weights_split folder from Google Drive . Place its contents in a weights_split/ folder at the root of the cloned repository , producing this layout: napari-omniem/ # the cloned repository root ├── pyproject.toml # (already present) editable-install target ├── README.md # (already present) ├── src/ # (already present) the plugin source └── weights_split/ # (you create this) place the downloaded files here ├── backbone_4246a479.pt # shared ViT-L backbone (~1.2 GB) ├── head_denoise-emdiffuse-l.pt ├── head_superreso-emdiffuse-l.pt ├── head_mito-seg-ViT-L-2D.pt └── head_mito-seg-ViT-L-3D.pt weights_split/ belongs next to pyproject.toml , src/ , and README.md at the repository root, not inside src/ . If those files are its siblings, the folder is in the correct location. You can change this folder later under Preferences → Settings → Weights storage folder . When you save a new location, the plugin offers to move your existing managed weights there. See the Preferences reference and Backbone management . 4. Launch napari After napari starts, open Plugins and select OmniEM . Troubleshooting PyQt6 conflict. This plugin uses PyQt5. If PyQt6 was pulled into the environment by a previous install and napari fails to start with a Qt binding error, remove it and reinstall: pip uninstall -y PyQt6 PyQt6-Qt6 PyQt6-sip || true Linux / Wayland. If the napari window fails to open (blank window or an xcb or OpenGL platform error), set the Qt platform for this environment. You can then start the application with the standard napari command: conda env config vars set QT_API=pyqt5 QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=glx conda activate napari-omniem # re-activate to apply Notes Ensure your GPU drivers and CUDA runtime are installed before installing PyTorch with CUDA support. Large-volume inference needs sufficient GPU memory and disk space. Multi-GPU inference is supported when multiple CUDA devices are available.

docs.text: Task, solution, and backbone management Napari-OmniEM lets you manage tasks, solutions, and shared model backbones from the GUI. Open ⚙️ Preferences → Tasks and Models , then select Solutions or Backbones . This page covers persistent model management : saved task configurations, solution registrations, backbone registrations, and managed weight files. It is separate from unloading active models from GPU or CPU memory in the current napari session. Concepts Relationship to the omniem package omniem is the core Python package that defines the OmniEM model architecture, shared-backbone and task-head structure, model loading, and model-config schema. Napari-OmniEM builds its task and solution management interface on these concepts. The model configuration YAML selected in Add Solution follows omniem.config.ModelConfig and is parsed by the omniem package; the plugin then adds its own task registration, persistence, and GUI metadata. A Task defines the problem type: Image-to-Image (for example, denoising or super-resolution) or Image-to-Label (for example, mitochondria segmentation). A Solution is a specific model and configuration that solves a task. A task may hold several solutions; each solution belongs to exactly one task. A Backbone is the shared encoder used by one or more solutions. Each solution also has a smaller, task-specific head. Managing tasks New Task Click New Task and provide: Task Type : Image-to-Image or Image-to-Label . Full Name : the name shown in the GUI selection menus (must be unique). Short Name : a concise identifier used to store the task's config file (must be unique). For an Image-to-Label task, also define each output label and its meaning. Each label corresponds to one model output class. Enable / Disable Task Select a task, then use Enable Task / Disable Task (only the applicable one is active). A disabled task does not appear in the in-memory or local inference menus. Its solutions remain saved and reappear when you re-enable the task. Delete Task Delete Task permanently removes a task and its config. If the task's solutions have head files in the managed weights folder, the plugin asks whether to delete or keep those files. This action never deletes the shared backbone. Dump Task / Import Task (sharing) To move an entire task between installations: Dump Task writes only the task description : a .yaml file listing its solutions. It does not copy weights. Import Task reads that .yaml file and registers the task under a unique short name that you provide. You also select the folder containing the weight files. Because Dump Task writes only the description, sharing a task requires both the dumped YAML and the weight files: Dump Task → get mytask.yaml . Export Weights for each solution into a folder; see Export Weights . Send the YAML + the weights folder. The recipient uses Import Task , selects the YAML, points at the weights folder, and gives a unique short name. Head files must match the YAML Every solution's head file must be present in the selected weights folder and its filename must match the name recorded in the dumped YAML. If you renamed a Split export, update the YAML (or re-export) so the names line up, otherwise the importer cannot find the weights. Managing solutions Add Solution Use Add Solution to import a compatible, fine-tuned OmniEM model into the selected task. Before continuing, prepare the model-config and weight files described in Custom model requirements . Open Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Solutions . Select the task that the model belongs to, then click Add Solution . Select the model config ( .yaml ). Its parsed contents are displayed as read-only so that you can confirm the architecture, task type, output-channel count, and normalization settings. Choose an import strategy: Full-scale (.pt) imports a complete checkpoint. The plugin splits it into a shared backbone and task head. It reuses an already registered matching backbone; otherwise, you can assign the new backbone a display name. Head-only (split .pt) imports a compatible head file. Select the matching registered backbone that the head requires. Select the weights file and confirm. The plugin validates the artifacts, copies the head into the managed weights folder, and registers the solution. If the import is rejected The plugin validates the model before committing the solution. Common messages include: Message Meaning Unsupported model or encoder The config uses an architecture or encoder that this Napari-OmniEM version does not support. Task type mismatch The config's task type does not match the selected task. Label count mismatch An Image-to-Label model's output-channel count does not match the task's labels. Backbone or encoder mismatch The head and selected backbone are incompatible. Head file validation failed The head lacks the required metadata or was created for a different backbone. Solution metadata cannot be changed after a solution is added. To change it, remove the solution and add it again. Remove Solution Select a solution and click Remove Solution . If the solution's head file is in the managed weights folder, you can delete the file , keep it , or cancel . Removing a solution deletes it from the task config; a shared backbone is never removed by this action. Export Weights Select a solution and click Export Weights , then choose an output format: Combined writes one self-contained .pt file containing the backbone and head. Split writes separate backbone and head files. This format avoids sharing another copy of a backbone that the recipient already has. To share a complete task, export the weights for each solution and use the Dump Task / Import Task procedure. Managing backbones Every solution uses a shared backbone , a large encoder such as EM-DINO ( EMDINOv1-ViTL ), plus a smaller task-specific head. A backbone is loaded once and reused by every solution that references it, reducing GPU memory use. Open Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Backbones to manage the backbone registry. Backbone inventory The Backbones table lists one row per registered backbone: Column Meaning Display Name A friendly name, which defaults to the tag. Tag A short content fingerprint that identifies the weights. Arch The encoder architecture, such as emdinov1 . Solutions The number of task heads that reference the backbone. Actions Rename and Remove actions for the backbone. The built-in backbone ( 4246a479 , EMDINOv1-ViTL ) is always registered, and its Remove action is disabled. Rename changes only the display name, up to 64 characters. It does not change the backbone tag. Add a backbone Click + Add Backbone , then choose one of these methods: Register split .pt selects a standalone backbone that has already been split from a checkpoint. The file is copied into the managed weights folder and registered. Extract from combined .pt selects a full checkpoint. The backbone is extracted, stored, and registered without modifying the original file. Remove a backbone The effect of Remove depends on the backbone: A built-in backbone cannot be removed. Removal is blocked while a model is loaded on the backbone or a solution references it. Unload the model or remove the referencing solutions first. An external file , stored outside the managed weights folder, is removed from the registry without deleting the physical file. For an unreferenced managed file , you can delete the file or remove only its registry entry. This is persistent removal Preferences → Backbones → Remove changes the persistent backbone registry and can optionally delete the weight file. Unloading an active backbone from session memory is a separate operation and does not change the registry or its files. Backbone settings Configure these options under Preferences → Settings → General settings ; see the Preferences reference : Weights storage folder controls where the plugin stores managed backbone_<tag>.pt and head_*.pt files. When you change the folder, the plugin offers to move the existing managed files. Backbone cache size controls how many distinct backbones may remain loaded at once. Best practices Use descriptive task and solution names. Dump a task (and export its weights) before major changes. Keep your weights in the managed weights storage folder so the plugin can find and move them for you. docs.text: Preferences reference The ⚙️ Preferences button opens the settings dialog. It has two tabs: Settings (defaults and software-wide options, described here) and Tasks and Models (see Task, solution, and backbone management and Custom model requirements ). Changes made here do not require a restart. Creating a task does require one; the interface indicates this when applicable. Inference defaults Change and save these values to define your own default inference settings. The saved values become the starting settings for future runs, but you can still override them for an individual run in the in-memory Advanced settings or the on-disk wizard. Setting Notes Device Default compute device ( cpu or cuda:N ). Batch size Tiles processed together. Default 4 . XY input size Square tile size fed to the model. Default 224 (range 112–896, step 112). Overlap Fractional overlap between tiles. Default 0.25 . Blend mode How overlapping tiles are combined, constant or gaussian . Normalization source scan-data (whole-volume statistics) or model (the model's built-in statistics). See Sliding window parameters below for what each of the tiling parameters does. Sliding window parameters Sliding-window inference tiles a large image into overlapping windows, runs each through the model, and merges the results. It is used by both in-memory (tiled) and on-disk inference. The values above are the defaults; each has a per-run override (the Advanced section in-memory, or the wizard on-disk). Input XY size The spatial size, in pixels, of each window in the XY plane. Larger windows provide more context and usually better quality; smaller windows use less GPU memory but can weaken boundary consistency. The default is 224 , with a range of 112–896 in steps of 112 . Use the largest size that fits in GPU memory. Batch size The number of windows processed together in one forward pass. Larger batches increase throughput; smaller batches use less GPU memory. The default is 4 . Set it to 1 when GPU memory is limited, then increase it gradually. Overlap The fractional overlap between adjacent windows ( 0.0 to 0.5 ). Greater overlap smooths boundaries and reduces stitching artifacts but is slower. The default is 0.25 . Lower it toward 0.1 for speed on tolerant Image-to-Image runs, and keep it higher for boundary-sensitive Image-to-Label tasks. Blend mode The method used to merge overlapping tiles: constant (uniform) or gaussian (weighted toward tile centers, smoother seams). Practical tips Prefer larger XY sizes over larger batch sizes for better quality. Keep overlap ≥ 0.1 to avoid visible stitching artifacts. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error occurs, reduce the batch size first, then the XY input size. Reduce the overlap only as a last resort. See Inference Tips & Common Pitfalls for memory usage, out-of-memory recovery, and scratch-disk guidance. General settings Software-wide options. Weights storage folder Where the plugin keeps its managed weight files ( backbone_<tag>.pt and head_*.pt ). Use Browse… to change it; the plugin offers to move the existing managed files to the new folder so your models keep working. Backbone cache size How many distinct shared backbones may stay resident in memory at once. Because tasks share a backbone, a small cache is usually enough; raise it only if you switch between models that use different backbones. GPU and CPU memory limits The GPU (VRAM) limit and CPU (RAM) limit settings cap how much memory a run may use. Each setting has: A source: Auto (half of the device's total memory), Custom (the MB value in the spinbox), or Off (no limit). A mode: Hard or Soft . Hard blocks a run when its upper-end memory estimate exceeds the cap; Soft only warns and lets you continue. “Proceed anyway” Before a run, the plugin estimates the memory it needs. If that estimate cannot be guaranteed—because it exceeds a soft limit or because the available GPU memory or scratch space is insufficient—you see a Proceed anyway option. It lets you run at your own risk; the run may still hit an out-of-memory error. Use the buttons at the bottom to Save or Reset all settings, or to Close the dialog. docs.text: Tools Workbench (🧰) The 🧰 More Tools button on the OmniEM toolbar opens a workbench of utilities that sit alongside the main inference panel. It has six tabs. Memory Management Memory Management operates only on active models loaded in the current napari session . Use it to load, measure, and unload runtime model objects while monitoring GPU and host memory. These actions do not remove saved tasks or solutions, deregister backbones, or delete model weight files. The readout shows the resident backbone and its reference count, the loaded heads, allocated, reserved, and free GPU memory, and host RAM use. Each unload action reports how much memory it freed. Button What it does Preload Load the selected solution now to make the first run faster. Profile this solution Measure the solution's actual memory use. This is not a passive inspection : profiling may evict loaded models and perform GPU forward passes. Remove Unload the selected active solution head from memory. Its saved solution and weights remain unchanged. Remove backbone Unload the active shared backbone when no loaded model references it. Its registration and weight file remain unchanged. Clear all models Unload every active head and backbone without changing saved model definitions or files. Clear temporal data Delete on-disk inference scratch files (see the warning below). Refresh Update the memory readout. Clear temporal data affects open results On-disk inference results stay backed by their scratch file while you view them. Clear temporal data deletes those files immediately, which can make still-open result layers unreadable. Save anything you need first. File Management File Management is a standalone checkpoint-conversion tool: Split converts one combined checkpoint into separate backbone and head files. Merge combines a backbone and head into one checkpoint. These operations work directly on the selected files. They do not add a solution or change the task, solution, or backbone registries. Pre-process Reserved for input pre-processing tools. Coming soon. Post-process Image-to-Image : rescale a model output's intensity back to the input's range. Pick the original image (the intensity reference) and the model output; optionally replace the output layer in place. This is the recommended final step after an Image-to-Image run. Image-to-Label : reserved for label post-processing. Coming soon. Related pages Inference Persistent task, solution, and backbone management Preferences Custom model requirements
